Manuscript draft. Readers are assumed to be familiar with Gomaa et al. [1].

2Problem formulation

2.1Motivation

Hybrid simulation relies on the transfer system to impose the computed displacements on the specimen. When the outer controller loop loses stability, the actuator drives the specimen far beyond its intended response. Such instability creates safety hazards for laboratory personnel. In addition, it can damage the specimen and expensive equipment such as the actuator and servo-valve. An unstable test is also usually terminated early, so the experiment fails and must be repeated with a new specimen. Maghareh et al. [2] noted that a failure in part of the physical substructure can drastically change its dynamics. They also noted that such a change affects the safety and integrity of the experiment.

Gomaa et al. [1] showed that specimen degradation can cause this instability. As the specimen degrades, its stiffness decreases and the same control action produces a larger response. The resulting gain amplification reduces the stability margin of the outer controller loop. However, that finding was obtained from a virtual hybrid simulation. This section therefore examines whether the same mechanism appears in a physical experiment.

2.2Experimental setup

Figure 1 shows the experimental setup. The specimen is a steel column. Its base is anchored to a concrete block with four Hilti anchors, and its top is connected to the actuator. An MTS hydraulic actuator with a capacity of 10 kip imposes the lateral displacement at the top of the column. The internal LVDT of the actuator measures this displacement. A Speedgoat real-time target sends the command to the actuator at 2048 Hz.

Damage is introduced through the anchorage. As the specimen is pushed, the concrete around the anchors cracks. This cracking is an early stage of concrete breakout. The breakout cone did not form, and the cracks were not yet visible, so the damage is partial. The base nevertheless loses part of its rotational stiffness. Consequently, the lateral stiffness at the actuator control point decreases.

No numerical substructure is involved in the tests of this section. The reference u(t) is a prescribed displacement, so only the outer controller loop is closed. Figure 2 shows this loop. The outer controller C(s) acts on the tracking error u(t)−y(t) and sends the command v(t) to the plant H(s,k). The measured displacement y(t) is then fed back to the controller.

2.3Initial and damaged systems

The plant H(s,k) was identified in two specimen states. In the initial state, the lateral stiffness of the specimen was k0=7.20 MN/m. After the anchorage was damaged, the lateral stiffness fell to 5.38 MN/m, or 0.75k0. The two plants are denoted H0 and Hd hereafter.

In each state, band-limited white noise up to 80 Hz was applied through the loop of Figure 2 with the same C(s). The transfer function from the command v(t) to the measured displacement y(t) was then estimated between 0.1 and 80 Hz. Frequencies with coherence below 0.8 were excluded. A parametric model was fitted to each estimate, with five poles for H0 and six for Hd.

2.4Effect of degradation on stability

Consider again the loop of Figure 2. The controller C(s) is the same in both states, and only the specimen changes. The open-loop transfer function is therefore L0=CH0 in the initial state and Ld=CHd in the damaged state. Figure 3 compares the two frequency responses and the chordal distance used by the NCF margin.

The 25% loss of lateral stiffness raised the loop gain by a factor of about 2.4 below 10 Hz. However, the phase of the loop changed by less than 4° in this range. The loss of stiffness therefore mainly amplifies the loop gain rather than adding phase lag. Consequently, the chordal distance dips near 35–38 Hz, and the NCF margin falls from 0.59 to 0.34. Table 1 summarizes the two states. The damaged margin is below the 0.4 guideline recommended by Gomaa et al. [1]. These trends agree with the gain-amplification mechanism reported in [1]. They also support the assumption in Section 3.1.2 that degradation scales the open-loop gain by a real factor g.

2.5Problem statement

These results expose a dilemma for a fixed outer controller. A controller tuned for the initial state becomes too aggressive once the specimen degrades. Conversely, a controller tuned for the damaged state sacrifices tracking in the initial state. The specimen state is also unknown during the experiment. The stability of the outer controller loop must therefore be quantified online from the available measurements. The controller must then be updated accordingly so the experiment is completed safely and successfully. Section 3 presents a framework that meets both requirements.

3Online NCF stability indicator framework for adaptive control

The NCF online stability indicator (NCF OSI), proposed by Gomaa et al. [1], quantifies the robustness of the closed-loop system as the physical plant changes during the experiment. The study showed that specimen stiffness degradation can drive the outer controller loop toward instability through a gain-amplification mechanism. In this study, we extend the analytical results to experimental implementation, discuss the challenges that arise, and propose ways to address them. The proposed framework comprises two parts: an online estimator of the indicator and an adaptive controller that gets updated accordingly. The indicator is estimated during the experiment from the desired displacement calculated by the numerical substructure and the measured actuator displacement by combining three estimator branches at each frequency, each weighted by the confidence in its output. The first is direct identification, bid, which estimates the closed-loop transfer function of the outer controller loop from the desired displacement u(t) to the measured actuator displacement y(t), with the H1 cross-spectral estimator [3]. The second is output-power inference, bpow, which can detect loop amplification at frequencies that cannot be reliably identified. This branch compares the output power measured during the experiment against the reference recorded before the excitation. The third is the prior identification of the initial state, b0, which serves as a fallback when insufficient information is available. The adaptive controller then uses the estimated indicator to scale the controller output by the adaptive factor λ, keeping the loop stable with an adequate margin as the specimen degrades while retaining as much tracking performance as possible. This section presents the framework and then its calibration.

3.1Framework Architecture

In the hybrid simulation block diagram shown in Figure 4, the numerical substructure computes the desired displacement d(t) from the ground acceleration and measured force fm(t). To compensate for transfer-system lag and improve tracking, a phase-lead compensator receives d(t) and produces the reference u(t). The outer controller C(s) takes the tracking error u(t)−y(t), where y(t) is the measured actuator displacement. It scales its output by the adaptive factor λ∈(0,1] to produce the command v(t) sent to the plant H(s,k).

The plant comprises the transfer system and the specimen of stiffness k. The transfer system includes the inner-loop controller, servo-valve, and actuator. The control–structure interaction between the actuator and specimen is also included in the transfer-system dynamics. The measured force fm(t) is fed back to the numerical substructure and closes the numerical substructure loop, while the measured displacement y(t) is fed back to the outer controller, closing the outer-controller loop.

The NCF OSI block runs alongside the outer-controller loop and does not alter the signals within it. It collects the reference u(t) and the measured displacement y(t) over a moving window and estimates the NCF margin of the current loop at each update. The adaptive law then compares this estimate with a target margin and updates the adaptive factor λ. A lower margin reduces λ to restore stability, while a sufficient margin lets λ recover toward one to retain tracking performance.

The plant in Figure 4 is characterized by the transfer function H(s,k)=Y(s)/V(s) from the command v(t) to the measured actuator displacement y(t). The open-loop transfer function and closed-loop response from u(t) to y(t) are

L(s,λ,k)=λC(s)H(s,k),
(1)
T(s,λ,k)=Y(s)U(s)=L(s,λ,k)1+L(s,λ,k),
(2)

Here U(s) and Y(s) are the Laplace transforms of u(t) and y(t). The NCF stability margin of the outer controller loop is evaluated for the loop L under unity feedback [4]:

bNCF(L)=infω|1+L(jω)|2(1+|L(jω)|2).
(3)

As the specimen changes during a hybrid simulation, the loop L(jω) changes with it. Equation (3) could be applied directly only if L(jω) were identified with high confidence at every frequency, but online measurements rarely support this across the full band. The NCF OSI is therefore estimated from three complementary branches, direct identification bid, output-power inference bpow and prior identification of the initial state b0, which the following sections develop in turn.

3.1.1Direct identification branch, bid

Identifying the closed-loop transfer function requires the autospectrum of reference u(t) and the cross spectrum of measured actuator displacement y(t) with u(t). The autospectrum of y(t) is also needed to calculate coherence, which helps set the confidence weight at each frequency. A moving window lets these spectra follow changes in the specimen during the experiment.

Each window contains N=fsTw samples of u(t) and y(t), where fs is the sampling frequency and Tw is the window duration. Updates occur at intervals Δt, so consecutive windows overlap when Δt<Tw. The update index is n, and r=0,…,N−1 indexes samples within each window. The Hann-windowed discrete Fourier transforms are

Un(ωm)=∑r=0N−1w[r]un[r]e−j2πmr/N,
(4)
Yn(ωm)=∑r=0N−1w[r]yn[r]e−j2πmr/N,
(5)

where un[r] and yn[r] are the samples of window n, and ωm=2πmfs/N is the angular frequency of bin m. The samples of each window are weighted by the Hann window presented by Blackman and Tukey [5]:

w[r]=12[1−cos(2πrN−1)].
(6)

Welch [6] proposed estimating the power spectrum by averaging, with equal weight, the squared Fourier magnitudes of overlapping windowed segments of a record. Cross spectra are estimated in the same way from products of paired Fourier transforms, with one transform conjugated. In the present study, the plant changes as the specimen degrades, so recent windows should carry more weight than earlier ones. Each window therefore provides one raw estimate of the autospectra of u and y and the cross spectrum of y with u:

puu,n(ωm)=|Un(ωm)|2,
(7)
pyy,n(ωm)=|Yn(ωm)|2,
(8)
pyu,n(ωm)=Yn(ωm)Un*(ωm),
(9)

where the superscript * denotes the complex conjugate. These raw estimates are averaged with the geometric moving average proposed by Roberts [7], which updates an average from its previous value and the newest observation. Earlier spectra are retained, but their contributions decay as new windows arrive. This reduces scatter between updates while still following changes in the plant. The first complete window initializes the average. At each subsequent update, ηs weights the new spectrum and 1−ηs weights the previous average:

p¯uu,n(ωm)=(1−ηs)p¯uu,n−1(ωm)+ηspuu,n(ωm),
(10)
p¯yy,n(ωm)=(1−ηs)p¯yy,n−1(ωm)+ηspyy,n(ωm),
(11)
p¯yu,n(ωm)=(1−ηs)p¯yu,n−1(ωm)+ηspyu,n(ωm).
(12)

The NCF OSI is evaluated over Ω, the set of frequencies considered in the analysis.

At each selected frequency, the loop response can be identified directly from the reference u and the measured response y. The averaged spectra give the H1 estimate of the closed-loop frequency response [3] and the magnitude-squared coherence

T^n(jω)=p¯yu,n(ω)p¯uu,n(ω),
(13)
γn2(ω)=|p¯yu,n(ω)|2p¯uu,n(ω)p¯yy,n(ω).
(14)

Inverting Equation (2) gives the identified loop:

L^n(jω)=T^n(jω)1−T^n(jω).
(15)

Here, the identified loop is smoothed with the running median over neighbouring frequencies discussed by Di Matteo et al. [8], so the median is taken over each frequency and its two neighbours. The smoothed loop L^s,n is hence given by

L^s,n(jωm)=mediani∈{m−1,m,m+1}L^n(jωi).
(16)

The identified margin then follows from Equation (3):

bid,n=bNCF(L^s,n).
(17)

The quality of this estimate varies with time and frequency for two reasons. First, the command can be too weak for the measured response to rise above the sensor noise. Second, even an active command concentrates its energy in a limited band set by the ground motion and the structural modes, so bins outside that band carry little information.

Each bin therefore receives an identification weight wid,n between zero and one, built from three factors. The first is command activity An, detected from the root mean square of the window:

An={1,RMS(un)>ηAσu,0,otherwise,
(18)

where RMS(un) is the root mean square of the command samples in the considered window n, σu is the standard deviation of the command noise measured in a quiet record, and ηA is a hyperparameter to be tuned. The second factor is the input leverage ℓn, which reduces the weight of bins that carry little command energy. The command power in each bin is first normalized by its maximum over Ω:

ℓraw,n(ω)=p¯uu,n(ω)maxν∈Ωp¯uu,n(ν).
(19)

The raw leverage cannot serve as the weight directly. It is proportional to the bin power, so a bin with one tenth of the peak power would receive one tenth of the weight even though its estimate is still reliable. The weight should instead stay close to one while a bin carries enough command power and fall toward zero only when it carries too little. The hyperparameter ℓfloor sets this boundary:

ℓn(ω)=ℓraw,n(ω)ℓraw,n(ω)+ℓfloor,
(20)

which stays close to one in bins with ℓraw,n≫ℓfloor and decreases smoothly toward zero in bins with ℓraw,n≪ℓfloor. A bin with command power equal to ℓfloor times the peak receives half weight. The third factor is the coherence, which completes the weight

wid,n(ω)=Anγn2(ω)ℓn(ω).
(21)

This weight sets the share of this branch in the fusion of Section 3.1.3.

3.1.2Output-power inference branch

Direct identification fails when the command is weak or does not excite the relevant frequency band. Even then, a degrading specimen can still drive the system toward instability. However, the change in output power relative to the initial state can reveal loop amplification even at frequencies without strong excitation. This change therefore provides a second source of evidence for a reduction in the stability margin. This method is inspired by Wu and Wang [9], who used active-power deviation and its rate of change to discriminate changes in the transient operating regime of a virtual synchronous generator. To quantify this change, the averaged output power is compared with its initial reference:

qobs,n(ω)=p¯yy,n(ω)pyy,0(ω),
(22)

where qobs,n is the observed power ratio, which measures the change in output power at each frequency relative to the initial state. The averaged autospectrum of y is p¯yy,n from Equation (11), and pyy,0 is the reference autospectrum of y recorded in the initial state.

The output-power branch detects a change by comparing the present output power with a reference from the initial state. A single window of output power fluctuates strongly, so a reference taken from one window could bias every later comparison. The reference autospectrum is therefore the median of three raw autospectra recorded in the initial state. These are taken at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 s, with λ=1:

pyy,0(ω)=med{pyy,n1(ω),pyy,n2(ω),pyy,n3(ω)},
(23)

where n1, n2 and n3 are the corresponding updates. The median discards one unusually loud or quiet window.

According to the observation discussed in Gomaa et al. [1] and the experimental verification presented in Section 2.4, the change due to specimen degradation can be represented by an amplification g of the open-loop gain. Consequently, a candidate loop λngL0 predicts the ratio

qmodel,n(ω,g)=|1+L0(jω)1+λngL0(jω)|2,
(24)

where qmodel,n is the predicted power ratio, and L0(jω)=C(jω)H0(jω) is the loop of the prior identification of the initial state. The amplification is then selected as the candidate in 𝒢 that minimizes the logarithmic difference between the observed and predicted ratios:

g^n(ω)=arg ming∈𝒢|logqobs,n(ω)−logqmodel,n(ω,g)|,
(25)

where g^n is the selected amplification, and 𝒢 is a grid of candidate values of g.

The predicted ratio in Equation (24) assumes that only the loop has changed since the reference was recorded. At frequencies without excitation, however, the output consists mainly of sensor noise. Its power is estimated from few windows and therefore scatters. The reference is also the median of only three windows. Consequently, g^n can indicate an amplification that does not exist, and the estimated margin would decrease without degradation.

The identified margin bid,n cannot correct this error, because it is valid only at the excited frequencies. Degradation, however, changes the loop at all frequencies. At the excited frequencies, it appears as an increase in the magnitude of the identified loop. Section 2.4 observed such an increase by a factor of about 2.4. A real amplification inferred from output power should therefore be accompanied by an increase in the identified loop. The factor ρn measures this increase and thus confirms whether the amplification indicated by g^n is real.

The factor ρn is the real scale that best fits the prior loop λnL0 to the identified loop L^n in the weighted least-squares sense:

ρn=arg minρ∈ℝ∑ω∈Ωwid,n2(ω)|L^n(jω)−ρλnL0(jω)|2.
(26)

The factor is real, consistent with the real amplification g in Equation (24). Each term of the sum expands as

|L^n−ρλnL0|2=|L^n|2−2ρRe{λnL0*L^n}+ρ2|λnL0|2.
(27)

Setting the derivative with respect to ρ to zero gives

ρn=Re{∑ω∈Ωwid,n2(ω)λnL0*(jω)L^n(jω)}∑ω∈Ωwid,n2(ω)|λnL0(jω)|2.
(28)

The weight wid,n lets the well-identified excited frequencies dominate. The identified loop L^n is taken before frequency-median smoothing. For an unchanged specimen ρn≈1, whereas for the damaged specimen of Section 2 ρn≈2.4.

The confirmation cn sets how much the amplification inferred from output power is trusted. It depends on the loop increase ρn identified at the excited frequencies:

cn=ρn−1ρth−1,cn∈[ϵ,1],
(29)

where ρth is the confirmation threshold. Once ρn reaches ρth, cn equals one, and the amplification inferred from output power is fully trusted. The lower bound ϵ=0.1 is a safety minimum. It accounts for amplification that cannot be observed at any excited frequency, such as amplification from unmodeled dynamics or higher-mode effects. The accepted amplification is

g~n(ω)=1+cn(g^n(ω)−1),
(30)

where g~n replaces g^n in the averaging equation, Equation (31).

The accepted amplification at update n inherits the scatter of qobs,n and therefore varies between updates. To reduce this scatter while following the degrading specimen, successive accepted amplifications are averaged recursively. As for the spectra in Equations (10)–(12), more weight is placed on recent values. The average is formed on a logarithmic scale:

logg^s,n(ω)=(1−ηg)logg^s,n−1(ω)+ηglogg~n(ω),
(31)

where g^s,n is the smoothed amplification, and ηg is the averaging factor that weights the newest accepted amplification. Equation (3) then gives the margin of this branch:

bpow,n=bNCF(λng^s,nL0),
(32)

where bpow,n is the output-power margin.

An unconfirmed amplification should also carry little weight in the fused margin. The confirmation cn therefore also weights this branch, together with the identification weight:

wpow,n=(1−wid,n)cn,
(33)

where wpow,n is the weight of the output-power branch, and wid,n is the identification weight from Equation (21). Consequently, this branch receives the share left by direct identification, in proportion to the confirmation.

Unlike direct identification, which reflects both losses and gains in the stability margin, the output-power branch detects only open-loop gain amplification. Consequently, once the adaptive controller restores stability and the output power returns to its initial level, this branch cannot reflect a recovered loop. A recovery step is therefore introduced. While the median of qobs,n over Ω remains below one, the smoothed amplification is reduced gradually:

logg^s,n(ω)=rglogg^s,n−1(ω),
(34)

where rg is the recovery factor, with 0<rg<1. The reduction stops once the output power rises above its initial reference. As a result, the output power itself limits how far the amplification is released.

3.1.3Per-frequency fusion and reported indicator

The third branch is the margin of the prior identification of the initial state, evaluated with the current adaptive factor:

b0,n=bNCF(λnL0).
(35)

At each frequency, the three branches now provide three margin estimates, which are combined according to the evidence behind each. The prior receives the weight left by the two measured branches:

w0,n=(1−wid,n)(1−cn).
(36)

The three margins are then combined with these weights at each frequency bin:

βn(ω)=wid,nbid,n(ω)+wpow,nbpow,n(ω)+w0,nb0,n(ω).
(37)

Fusion is performed bin by bin, before any reduction over frequency, so margins evaluated at different frequencies are never combined. This choice also handles the idle case without special treatment. When the command is inactive, wid,n=0 in every bin. An unchanged loop then reads its gain-scaled prior, and a bin with a remembered change continues to report it.

To drive the adaptive controller, the fused curve is reduced to a single value. The NCF OSI margin is taken as the lowest value of βn over Ω:

bOSI,n=minω∈Ωβn(ω),
(38)

where bOSI,n is the NCF OSI margin at update n, and Ω is the set of frequencies considered in evaluating the NCF OSI. The adaptive law then uses it to update λn+1. Figure 5 summarizes one complete update, from the measured signals to the adaptive factor, and Table 2 lists the estimator parameters.

3.1.4Adaptive factor update

The NCF OSI estimated in Section 3.1.3 provides the margin needed to adjust the adaptive controller factor λ. When the margin falls below a specified target, λ is reduced to maintain the stability of the system. This reduction is intended to counteract the gain amplification caused by specimen degradation, as discussed earlier in Section 2.

To achieve this while retaining as much tracking performance as possible, λ is updated from the difference between the estimated margin and a target margin:

en=bOSI,n−btar,
(39)

where en is the margin error, and btar is the target NCF margin. A negative error indicates insufficient margin, and a positive error indicates spare margin.

Reducing and restoring the adaptive factor carry different risks. A slow reduction leaves the loop exposed while the margin is insufficient. Conversely, a fast recovery can raise λ back toward instability before the estimate settles. The adaptive factor is therefore reduced and restored at different rates:

λn+1={λnexp(κen),en<0,λnexp(μκen),en≥0,λn+1∈[λmin,1],
(40)

where μ=0.32 is the ratio of the recovery rate to the reduction rate. Consequently, λ falls at full rate when the margin is below the target and recovers about three times more slowly. The adaptation gain is κ, and λmin is the smallest permitted adaptive factor.

3.2Calibration

The framework of Section 3.1 contains 15 parameters, listed in Table 2. Seven of them are design values set by the test and the analysis. The window duration Tw and the update interval Δt are defined in Section 3.1.1. The window duration of 0.5 s gives a frequency resolution of 2 Hz, which also sets the lower bound of Ω. The update interval of 0.125 s sets how often the indicator and λ are updated. The upper bound of Ω, 80 Hz, matches the band over which the plants were identified in Section 2.3. The grid 𝒢 spans the amplifications expected from degradation. The target btar=0.4 follows the guideline of Gomaa et al. [1], and λmin keeps part of the controller active.

The remaining eight are hyperparameters. They set how quickly the indicator follows a change, how much evidence each branch requires, and how strongly the adaptive factor responds. Their values depend on the laboratory, the equipment, the specimen and its material. They therefore cannot be fixed from theory and must be calibrated against cases with a known margin.

The two plants identified in Section 2 provide such cases. Because both models are known, the true NCF margin can be computed at every update and compared with the estimate. To impose damage numerically, both models receive the same command v(t), and their outputs are mixed:

y(t)=[1−δ(t)]y0(t)+δ(t)yd(t),
(41)

where y0 and yd are the outputs of H0 and Hd, and δ(t)∈[0,1] is the damage index. Here δ=0 represents the initial state and δ=1 represents the damaged state. While δ is constant, superposition makes this mixture equivalent to the plant (1−δ)H0+δHd. The true margin therefore follows from Equation (3) applied to λC[(1−δ)H0+δHd]. The mixture interpolates the responses of the two states and does not represent an intermediate stiffness.

The calibration cases combine three features. The first is the damage history. Each case lasts 120 s. Sudden damage steps δ from zero to one at 40 s and back to zero at 80 s. Gradual damage ramps δ up between 20 and 50 s and back down between 70 and 100 s. The second feature is the excitation band. The reference u(t) is band-limited white noise with an RMS of 0.15 mm. Sensor noise with a standard deviation of 0.05 mm is added to the measured displacement.

Wideband excitation covers 2 to 80 Hz and therefore includes the frequencies of the minimum margin, near 35–38 Hz. Narrowband excitation covers only 2 to 10 Hz. Direct identification then cannot observe the change at those frequencies, and only output-power inference can detect it. The third feature is the adaptive factor. With λ fixed at one, the cases test whether the indicator estimates the margin correctly. With λ active, the same cases test whether the loop is held at the target while tracking is retained. Table 3 lists the resulting eight cases.

Figures 6 and 7 show the cases with λ fixed and active. Each column shows one case in three panels. The first shows the command and the measured displacement. The second shows the damage index δ. The third compares the estimated bOSI with the true margin and btar, and shows λ in the adaptive cases.

Four simple metrics summarize each case after the first 5 s. The estimation error is the mean of |bOSI−bNCF|. The roughness is the median of the second difference of bOSI, multiplied by 1000, so steady changes are not penalized. The travel is the total variation of λ, which measures how much the controller is adjusted. The unsafe time is the percentage of time with bNCF<btar−0.02. Table 4 lists the results.

Each case constrains particular hyperparameters. The wideband cases set the spectral averaging ηs, the activity threshold ηA and the leverage reference ℓfloor of direct identification. The narrowband cases set the output-power parameters. Their damage onset sets ρth and ηg, and their return to the initial state sets rg. The adaptive cases set the adaptation gain κ. The values in Table 2 were tuned on a wider benchmark, which also included a closed-loop experimental record and a replay of a recorded hybrid simulation. The eight cases above illustrate their behavior.

Appendix A. Assumptions and limitations

The estimator relies on four assumptions, and each one limits how the reported indicator should be interpreted.

  1. The identification branch assumes that the output disturbance is uncorrelated with u. Feedback through the numerical substructure can violate this assumption and bias T^n even at high coherence.
  2. The output-power branch assumes that the disturbance spectrum is unchanged from the reference period and that the first 1.5 s represent the initial loop at full gain. A change in disturbance intensity or in the command-driven response can therefore alter qobs without any change in stability.
  3. The factor g is real. The output-power branch therefore captures changes in loop magnitude but not in loop phase.
  4. Band limitation means that bOSI is not a guaranteed lower bound on the full-frequency margin bNCF, because frequencies outside Ω are not evaluated.
